rationale: Studies differ a lot in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so the same genus can sit at very different abundance levels in each study. I will standardize log relative abundance within each study (z-score per genus per study, no labels used) before the random forest. Then its splits follow how a genus differs from its own study's typical level, not how studies differ from each other.

IBD is known for lower gut microbial diversity, and a random forest that only sees per-genus z-scores cannot easily rebuild community-wide diversity from them. This change adds alpha-diversity features at OTU and genus level: Shannon, inverse Simpson, and depth-controlled Hurlbert rarefied richness. Hurlbert richness is exact and deterministic. All three are z-scored within study, like the genus features, so depth and protocol differences between studies are removed.

Every OTU without a named genus currently goes into a single `g__` bucket, so signal from unnamed genera in different families gets mixed together. That bucket includes many unclassified Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae and Enterobacteriaceae OTUs, which are central to IBD. This change adds family-level and phylum-level log relative abundances, z-scored within study like the other features. The forest can then use the well-known IBD shifts at family and phylum level: loss of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, and gain of Enterobacteriaceae and Proteobacteria. These higher levels should also be more consistent across studies than genus labels.

Many genera and families are present in only a few samples, so after within-study z-scoring they are mostly noise. With a √p feature sample at each split, these rare columns push informative ones out of the candidate set. This change drops any taxon whose prevalence is below 10% in every study (label-free filtering). The forest should then split more often on well-supported IBD taxa, and the change still keeps taxa that only one study detects.
